title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga is a game I'm quite torn on. While there are many aspects of the experience I absolutely adore, there is a large element to this game which I feel drags the experience down, making it not an immediate recommend I know it should be. To get to the best part of the game over with: presentation. The visuals are absolutely breathtaking and I found myself entranced playing through this game. Every character had personality oozing from their design alone and each boss you encounter feels lovingly thought of. [spoiler]I really felt this way about the Yellow and White Gods you see in the game. There is a sense of scale each of them have which does make you feel how daunting these 'Gods' are to our characters.[/spoiler] The visuals, alone, are not solely what carries this game. The music brought me into the world. Where many games I find enjoyable, but something I'm not going to think back on, Small Saga's soundtrack heightens the overall experience. The emotions are brought to another level when you play through, aiding to the story in more ways than you realize. From the lows to the highs, and the bosses through, the soundtrack assists in making a memorable presentation in the time you put in. The story is nothing amazing, but it's quite serviceable enough. The writing, overall, is enough to get you through. Yet I did find myself wanting more in. I would have loved more quests which allow you to learn more about the characters in the game. More people to interact with. I just found myself wanting more. The lore you do find in the books just feels a little clunky to me, making me just wish there was another manner to explore this world I'm shown. That said, the writing was enough to make me want to see more of this game. Now, the gameplay, which is where my experience takes a dip. It feels like the game focused on every other issue, yet the gameplay and everything surrounding it took a step back. Lacking is a word that immediately comes to mind, but even that might not properly do it justice. Despite the presentation and writing which all kept me coming in, the mechanics in the game was pushing me away. The game felt like it needed a vehicle to have their game, and made a passable RPG experience in order to do so. What is here was clearly given enough time to make it not completely arbitrary, yet not delved too deep into and allowing for a more fleshed out playthrough. For $20, this game is on the edge for me. Everything truly is incredible for this game, yet the game mechanics bring it down quite a bit for me. It takes what could easily have been a homerun and makes me more on the fence. Yet, if the game goes on sale at all, I would highly recommend picking this game up. Despite my feelings on the gameplay, Small Saga clearly had passion put behind it when it comes to presentation. And I think, if you can get past the mostly average mechanics, you do have a beautiful game awaiting you on the otherside.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga was pretty mediocre. There are some pretty cute moments where I enjoyed the characters and how they reacted to the events unfolding. However, the overall story operates at so much of a breakneck pace that it makes character development incredibly jarring; characters will flip motivation on a dime just to railroad the main plot. In the span of ~6 hours, you [spoiler] help a child run away from home, start a prison break which leads to overthrowing an authoritarian town and installing a new leader, start a revolution against the monarchy, overthrow a slaver, and help a person reconcile their past[/spoiler]. The game honestly tries to do too much too fast, which makes transitioning between main story beats turbulent. This results in characters not realistically offering pushback on others or having instantaneous changes of heart. Simultaneously, new ideas and information on people’s past are constantly introduced, but never meaningfully utilized or elaborated on. Many of the main story conflicts are resolved off screen and are only barely mentioned being resolved in a few sentences. A few characters are particularly loathsome with cringy dialogue in the form of forced memes. There are also several references to memes that were topical at the time. Constant attempts at humor are made but they mostly fall flat. The story takes up the vast majority of the game with some light amount of boss combat near the climax of each plot point. The combat is extremely vapid to the point it feels like a fantasy story masquerading as an RPG. There aren’t any meaningful decisions to make in terms of building character skills or gear. In fact, the game has several skills that increase damage to different types of enemies that either appear in only 2 combats or only in one chapter. I never felt in danger during combat and it boiled down to spamming damage abilities with no thought. It is very dissonant to be a meek rodent trying to rise up against larger creatures while combat is never dangerous. The final boss of the game was doing attacks that did 2 damage to me. There is a lack of polish that hampers the storytelling experience. Many important story moments had no music or ambient sound that made reading the dialogue emotionally hollow. Nearly every cutscene in the game used fades to black to hide actions being performed, items being placed, etc. There are also many incredibly long walkways between story areas that don’t serve any purpose to gameplay or storytelling. They don’t build atmosphere and just pad playtime as you meander through empty halls in dead silence. Overall, I found Small Saga to be entertaining enough to want to see the game through. The game was gifted to me and I think if I had spent the $15 myself, I would be more disappointed. For that reason, I can’t really recommend this game to others for its price. The plot is too hasty and needs to take more time so that many of the introduced threads are not hand waved away.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga is a wonderful bite of nostalgia. A tale reminiscent of an era of role playing games last seen on game consoles of old. Filled with classic character tropes, zany antics and comic mischief layered on top of darker themes. The game itself is not expansive, but what it lacks in exploration and experimentation it more than makes up for in humor, story-telling and presentation. The average play through would be equivalent to that of Final Fantasy or Dragon Warrior(Quest), the first in their respective series. But–I would argue that the story experience of this title will feel genuinely closer to that of Final Fantasy IV or Suikoden (the first.)

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga, in essence, isn't just a love letter to classic PSX-era JRPGs. There are moments in this game that brought me back to the same wide-eyed wonder that games like FFIX or Chrono Cross gave me as a child. A simple combat system, surprising exploration, lovable characters, the whole deal. The only real complaint I have for this game is I wish there were MORE. It's fitting that there isn't more, being called "Small Saga" and all, but a lot of the emotional climaxes just couldn't hit nearly as hard as something that had more space to breathe. It's all tightly, beautifully written, and it'll stick with me for a long while. I hope these devs continue to make games as wonderful as this.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: [h2]I'm Ashamed I Forgot About This Gem![/h2] You know that feeling of once playing through something fantastic, something that gave it its all with strong visual identity, memorable characters, and a story that genuinely sticks, only for it to slowly fade into the back of your mind years later? Well... I know that feeling well. That’s Small Saga. A JRPG that proves you do not need a massive open world to sell the idea of an incredible RPG. As even the smallest creatures have a big story to tell. [h2]Issue[/h2] Small Saga’s biggest issue was it's visibility. It released quietly and never quite got the spotlight it deserved, releasing around the same time that huge RPGs like (Baldurs Gate 3) were gaining traction. This of course made it easy to overlook or forget entirely. On top of that, I would have to say that a lot of people just don't like the idea of a linear RPG, you know, like myself. I prefer to overlevel and overexplore until I am a god, but here it's all on the rails story progression. Pacing can also feel somewhat quick, leaving some moments you wish had more time to breathe and fully come to life, but that's more on the small side. [h2]Impression[/h2] At its core, this is a classic JRPG. You manage a traditional party setup with a healer, support, and two fighters with some debuffs and buffs to help you on your journey. Progression is tied to boss fights, with a level gained after each one. For some players, this is where the experience can feel overly streamlined and, at times, unfun when you can't power level. This is similar to how a game like Chained Echoes handled progression, which was not fun. Combat itself is rarely challenging as long as you lean into the game’s powerful combo effects, which can make most encounters trivial. That lack of difficulty may leave some players underwhelmed. Where the game truly stands apart is its story, which is genuinely amazing. This is elevated even further by the pixelated, cinematic presentation during boss fights and key story moments. Those sequences are striking and memorable, and they do a lot of heavy lifting in setting the game apart from others in the genre. It's a solo developed masterpiece in every possible way. [h2]Story[/h2] You play as a small mouse in a vast, dangerous world. After your brother is killed by the Yellow God, you swear revenge and set out to end this particular humans tyranny. With your life destroyed, the rodent population of Rodentia lives in fear, until you march into the den of beasts on a quest far larger than you could realistically handle alone. Along the way, you grow stronger, learning from allies and experiences, as your journey shapes not only Verm, the sole survivor of the Yellow God’s reign, but also the other characters you encounter. The story emphasizes growth, resilience, and the bonds formed in the face of overwhelming odds, giving the narrative depth beyond the typical revenge tale. It's surprisingly emotional, and for once again a mostly solo-developed title, this is one such game you don't want to miss out on for various reasons. It's one of the best of it's kind. [h2]Conclusion[/h2] I’ve played through this game once and am now finishing a second full playthrough. I had completely forgotten how good it truly was. That’s the thing with games like this: no matter how memorable they were, over the years the impact of the story, character development, and world-building can gradually fade, but returning to them is like starting over fresh. You get to re-experience the joys of this world and appreciate for what it offers. Then one day, you decide to give it another try, expecting little more than a dull story because you personally feel bored of all the other games you have or haven't played, and suddenly you’re completely absorbed, hooked by the story, invested in the characters, and captivated by the presentation. So do yourself a favor: take a deep breath, stop hesitating, and pick up Small Saga. It’s an experience you won’t soon forget, unless you well... Forget like I did, over time. analysis_text: Ikenfell is a sweet little RPG I do like the game; the music is good, the story is nice. The gameplay left a bit to be desired, though. I found later-game activity to be rather frustrating and I ended up turning on easy mode; the two main grievances I have are routinely getting screwed over by the enemy party having too many turns in a row, and some actions, such as placing traps, not counting as a turn at all unless you do it. The last few sections of the game were so frustrating to me that they ended up souring the game in general a bit. I can't hold it against it too much, though: I'm not great at RPGs, and I don't like them much. Unfortunately many of the really good indie games seem to be RPGs. I'm not over the moon about this game but it's pretty good and probably worth your time, especially if you like this sort of game.

title: Ikenfell

It rewards careful positioning, and while the timing gimmick can start to feel tiresome after a while, each spell has a different timing to master, which keeps the combat fresh. title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: Great follow-up to To the Moon and another reminder that I really love these playable novel type games. What makes this one so fun is the mix of mystery and banter. I was always curious about what was really going on, what we were about to learn, and where the story was heading next. That kept me hooked the whole way through. At the same time, Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene make everything entertaining scene by scene, and Watts especially was a huge part of the fun for me with all his sarcasm, jokes, and random references. The low-friction interaction helps too, because the game stays focused on what it does best. The music and atmosphere were excellent! Now I’m really looking forward to Impostor Factory. I feel so lucky getting to play these all at once given these games originally came out years apart!

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: This is the second game in a trilogy that starts with To The Moon and ends with Impostor Factory. In my opinion, they should absolutely be played in order, so go play the first one if you haven't before even looking at this one. There's a lot of setup for the third game in this one, yet it still manages to tell a complete and satisfying story. This game also tells a much grander narrative than its predecessor, with higher quality writing. Definitely recommend it if you enjoyed the first one.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: This is the second-to-last game in the [i]To the Moon[/i] series. As with the previous titles, you can expect gorgeous pixel art, a beautiful soundtrack, expressive animations, and a lot of reading. Fortunately, the writing is top-notch. It leans far more toward a walking simulator than a traditional video game. In fact, Impostor Factory features even less player interaction than its predecessors. There are no more puzzles here at all. Instead, it focuses almost entirely on delivering its narrative. It is difficult for me to say which of the three main games I have liked the most so far. However, I can definitely say that Impostor Factory was the most emotionally impactful for me. The plot remained gripping all the way to the end, and the post-credits scene leaves plenty of room for speculation. I am glad there is still one more game left for me to play in this series. I guess I am just a sucker for these short, narrative-driven pixel art games.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: While some critics have pointed out that the story did not live to its "true potential", I personally think that for what it is; a story about finding meaning in an artificial world, it delivers its intended message exceptionally well. Impostor Factory doesn't need to be a complex sci-fi epic to be brilliant. It shows us that a physical reality doesn't really matter all that much. If you are feeling genuine love, grief or joy, then those emotions are 100% real to you in that moment. It's honestly my favorite so far from the series.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: Impostor Factory is interesting in that it challenges the philosophy presented in the previous games and sets up the Beach Episode for success by starting to put the hypocritical actions and beliefs of characters front and center. Also, compared to the other games, it also seems to focus a lot more closely on the emotions of the characters without them having to explicitly state how they were feeling. Characters cry and don't need to state why exactly they cry. You just know. I could notice that Kan Gao was making a clear effort to improve his writing and storytelling within Impostor Factory and, even if it isn't perfect, it still tells a cohesive story that can be enjoyed on its own. I also feel the need to pay some respects to Jordan Baer as this was the last game of the series that he was directly involved in (funny that his last game was very focused on being caught between living a normal life or a life dedicated to lighting the way for others). I hope his family is doing alright.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: Impostor Factory is significantly different to the first two To the Moon games, and it suffers for it. Unfortunately, I would consider this one to be the weakest of the series. To be clear, it is not a bad game, and it fits as an integral piece of the whole, but the level of captivation the other games manage in me is not quite achieved. I believe this is due to the change in protagonist, as Neil and Eva have next to no presence in the bulk of the story. They were what made the other games pop, with their funny, charming dialogue contrasting with the emotional weight of the others' stories, a sort of 'chiaroscuro' effect, if you will, that was incredible. As a part of the series, this is a must-play, but on its own, it has much to be desired. 6/10

It's difficult for me to rate this game strictly "recommended" or "not recommended" but I'll flag it as recommended since it's better than the vast majority of games I've played. I give Impostor Factory a 7 out of 10.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: [b]Impostor Factory[/b] serves as the missing link that finally brings the SigCorp saga together. While initially presented as a standalone murder mystery, it slowly reveals itself as a deeply connected narrative that ties [i]To the Moon[/i], [i]Finding Paradise[/i], and the minisodes into a single, coherent whole. What begins as an intriguing game gradually transforms into one of Kan Gao's most confident and emotionally resonant stories. Narratively, Impostor Factory feels like a return to form. The main theme is just as approachable as [i]Finding Paradise[/i] while having the same finesse in storytelling as [i]To the Moon[/i], taking the best of both worlds. The central twist was genuinely unpredictable to me, yet completely logical in hindsight, which is a very difficult balance to strike. The game also manages to expand [spoiler]Neil[/spoiler] as a character: questions that lingered across previous entries are addressed, adding layers of depth that recontextualize his behavior throughout the series. Overall, Impostor Factory feels like the perfect conclusion to a theoretical trilogy. It respects the legacy of the previous games while standing on its own, delivering one of the strongest narrative experiences in the series. [h1]The Good[/h1] + Perfectly ties together [i]To the Moon[/i], [i]Finding Paradise[/i], and the minisodes + Adds significant depth to [spoiler]Neil[/spoiler] and answers long-standing questions about him + Feels like a natural and satisfying conclusion to the trilogy + Storytelling is top tier, easily the strongest aspect of the game + Soundtrack and ambience are once again flawless + Plot twist manages to be the central piece that ties everything together while still being surprising + Baited by Kan Gao by thinking this was just a "murder mystery thriller featuring multiple casualties", unrelated to the past games + Still using the greatest game engine of all time, RPG Maker, to its full potential + We can finally run!! [h1]The Bad[/h1] - None. Well played. (first game I review where I have zero complaints, quite an achievement!) [i]Is it wrong if all I really wanted to be is just another lavender?[/i] [h2]10 / 10 - IGN[/h2]

title: To the Moon
analysis_text: Let me start by stating that I love pixel art, rich soundtracks, and narrative-driven titles. To the Moon checks all three boxes. I first played this game in 2018. While its beautiful soundtrack stayed with me over the years, most of the plot had faded from memory. During a recent multi-hour train ride, I was scrolling through my Steam Deck library and rediscovered this gem. I decided to give it another shot, playing through both the main game and the two free "Sigmund Minisodes" DLCs. There is so much to love here. It’s a deeply emotional story about life, love, family, and loss, following a dying man and his late wife, alongside two doctors who rarely agree on anything but always have each other's backs when it counts. The soundtrack, in particular, is stunning and carries the weight of the narrative effortlessly. Just don't expect traditional gameplay. The experience consists almost entirely of searching for objects, clicking through environments, and solving the occasional light puzzle. It leans far closer to an interactive visual novel or walking simulator than a standard video game. Because it's relatively short, it never overstays its welcome. For me, replaying it was an absolute pleasure. The optional minisodes also add a fantastic touch, fleshing out Sigmund Corp., exploring its employees, and leaving you with a few intriguing mysteries to chew on. If you enjoy story-driven experiences with great art and music, and don't mind minimal gameplay, you owe it to yourself to give To the Moon a try.

title: To the Moon
analysis_text: To the Moon is a great interactive game with an engaging story. It will leave you thinking about the fragility of life, and remind you to be grateful for everything you do have in your life. The art style is fitting for the atmosphere, and the premise is believable enough that you feel this could happen in our lifetimes. It’s not often I sit at the end of a game and say “wow”. This game did it for me. Give this game a try. It takes 3.5-5 hours to complete and you will unlock the single achievement once you complete the game. Go in blind, and enjoy the experience.

title: To the Moon
analysis_text: To the Moon sits in a very distinct category as far as games go. It is focused on story and emotion. The game mechanics are not important; you are not being punished for doing anything wrong during a puzzle, so leave your competitive side at the door when you press play. The game takes some ideas from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, but it still feels original. This comparison should give away the main concept of the game. If you loved the movie, I am sure you will also love this game. The music, composed by Kan Gao, also the creator of the game, is amazing. It fits the game perfectly; it never feels boring, even if you stay in the same scene for minutes. The songs have a calming, homey feel that never becomes annoying despite their repetition. The art matches the story; it always surprises me how pixel art can show a character's emotions so well. The colours remind me of autumn, and everything feels very atmospheric. It's a beautiful game to look at. I want to underline that, as with all different mediums of art, games can also have an emotional impact, and To the Moon will work your tear ducts to the maximum. Have some tissues ready, just in case.

It could also be that I don't connect as much with Colin as I do with Johnny (of course this could change with time.) It could even be that the funny banter between Neil and Eva somewhat breaks the pacing more in this entry compared to To The Moon. Even if it is a weaker entry, Finding Paradise will still find a way to make you cry and question your own existence and relationships. It might even give you a whole new way to look at your own reality. Who knows? It's the perfect opposite side of the coin to To The Moon in more ways than one.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: After getting my heart broken by To The Moon, I thought I was ready for its sequel, Finding Paradise. I was not. My heart is still broken all over again. Personally, I love To The Moon more because I think it have much impactful revelation in its story, but Finding Paradise still shines in its own way. [h3]STANDALONE SEQUEL[/h3] By the way, Finding paradise is a standalone sequel game for To The Moon. You dont need to play To The Moon first to understand Finding Paradise. However, I still advise you to play To The Moon first for much better experience. [h3]STORY[/h3] Finding Paradise carries a much darker theme compared to its prequel. While the storyline can be a bit predictable, the overall experience is still touching and well-written. Still managed to make me sobbing with the ending. [h3]GAMEPLAY[/h3] The gameplay is similar to its prequel. You need to interact with certain objects to establish memory links that allow you to go back in time. There are mini puzzles you need to solve every time you want to travel back in time. I appreciate the gamedev for trying to switch up the puzzles to make them different from the prequel, but personally, I prefer the old puzzles more. Spoiler: [spoiler]There is a boss fight in this game.[/spoiler] [h3]MAIN THEME[/h3] It’s hard to say much about this game without spoiling anything, but the main themes revolve around regret and acceptance. One thing I really like about this game, it kinda reveals how Sigmund Corp can be a double-edged sword. (Sigmund Corp is the company where the main characters work.) [h3]CONCLUSION[/h3] Please play this game if you want heartbreaking experience.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: [b]Finding Paradise[/b] continues SigCorp's story-driven formula by expanding on the world and characters introduced in [i]To the Moon[/i]. It once again places players in the role of Eva and Neil, navigating memories in order to fulfill a dying wish, with the focus once again set on narrative delivery rather than gameplay complexity. The structure will feel immediately familiar to anyone who has played the previous entry. The game's strongest element remains its writing. Dialogue is sharp, character-driven, and often emotionally grounded, with Eva and Neil continuing to carry much of the experience through their dynamic and interactions. The supporting cast is also well realized, and the game does a good job of fleshing out its characters through small, intimate moments. The music and atmosphere once again play a crucial role in setting the emotional tone. Overall, Finding Paradise is a high-quality narrative experience that maintains the emotional and technical standards set by [i]To the Moon[/i], even if it does not quite reach the same highs. While the story feels more predictable, the game is still a strong recommendation for fans of character-driven storytelling. [h1]The Good[/h1] + Always great to see more of Eva and Neil + Characters, dialogue, atmosphere and music are all top tier (Kan Gao is just flexing at this point lol) + RPG Maker games will always have a dear place in my heart + Navigation feels smoother, with fewer environmental elements blocking movement [h1]The Neutral[/h1] * I couldn't personally relate to the story as much - that said, the quality is still very high and I was moved at the end [h1]The Bad[/h1] - Main plot twist felt too obvious from the start [spoiler](that Feya only existed in his head)[/spoiler] - A run key is still missing - Lack of volume control options [i]All our memories are nothing but the fiction we tell ourselves[/i] [h2]9 / 10 - IGN[/h2]

analysis_text: So nice I bought it twice. After finishing the base game and DLC on PlayStation I decided it was time to move to some better hardware. The culmination of expert narrative construction, environmental storytelling and lore, awe inspiring vistas, mind blowing architecture, unparalleled gameplay, perfect sound design, epic score, staggering enemy variety including some of the coolest bosses in any FromSoft game to date with some of the most fascinating backstories and relationships. Not to mention an unbelievable amount of weapons, spells and armour to choose from to customise your Tarnished to your liking. The Soulsborne series has always been about overcoming adversity, and I don't think that's more present than in this game. It is genuinely overwhelming the sense of wonder and triumph this game provides, even on multiple playthroughs. Thank you Miyazaki and team, truly.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: Really crabbin' good but also real crabbin' long. I loved the writing, and the all of the party members were really memorable. Siffrin's gradual descent into madness was probably one of the most well-written explorations of time loops I've seen, and it had me telling myself to play just ONE MORE LOOP to find the differences, the things I couldn't interact with before. I do think that Act 3 and 4 dragged on in length, but at the same time I'm not sure I would have felt the same catharsis in Act 5 and 6 if it was shorter. Unfortunately my biggest gripe with this game is the way you get the true epilogue. Not using a useless, forgettable item multiple times should not be locking me out of the conclusion of arguably the second the most important character in the game, what the hell. Overall very well worth it -- if you have the patience for it.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: Easily one of the best takes on a time loop in a game. The writing does a perfect job of building a sense of hopelessness and existential dread the more times you reset. The setting is really cool and I wish it was explored more. The combat itself is a neat concept but becomes trivial during the back half of the game (probably intentional that doesn't mean it didn't drag the pacing down for me). Overall an excellent game and deserves a place among the great indie rpgs.

analysis_text: Final Update : Worse then I could have imagined. No pay off for the end. Final boss is a "out of no where" but also not really and it's a big let down. They gloss over any actual impact the end could have had for a non-offensive ending. If everyone in this world is gay, how do they keep the population? Come on guys, you want inclusion but you didn't actually have inclusion. That aside, the game-play is good and the only thing that carries the game. Seeing Ze and Zir is just so out of place. My theory was not correct but would have been a much better and dramatic ending, you know actual writing! Why is the last boss easier then the 2nd to last boss? The "lost sister" has no pay off and she doesn't deserve the happy ending she got because there was only a few scenes showing her that were there to make you think something else. I did call/predict the one twist that came true at the very very end after the credits. (Like I said predictable but also not predictable but in a very bad way) Oh and the end credits song... wow what a pile of ♥♥♥♥♥. Why did only a few of the characters get lyrics in their "theme song"... I could go on for paragraphs but I'll stop, it's not worth my time. I never give scores but for this I have to. Story 1/10 Game-play 9/10. Update 2 : Yet it still manages to be worse. I thought it was very predictable before and it just keeps NOT surprising me because I can tell what's going to happen. Also just about every other character is just so badly written and cookie cutter forced to be "non-conforming" it's laughable. I mean if you want to do inclusion at least TRY and be good about it. The game-play is the ONLY reason I'm still playing. Update : Oh god the writing got worse! At least the combat is fun. Mixed so far. Most of the characters are annoying and VERY cookie cutter stereotypes. Also why is it that everyone in the game has to be LGBT? Look, I'm an ally and all but come on, not everyone is "gender fluid". You want inclusion, I get that, that's great. However that also means you need some other types in there too. You go all in like that and it just feels forced. Also why are kids/very young teens constantly saying someone else is cute or hot? Needless to say the writing is pretty rough. Gameplay is ok so far. Some annoying enemies.

analysis_text: [b] 5 Point review [/b] 5 pros and 5 cons. Thumbs up or down is just my personal like or dislike of the game. title: Meg's Monster
analysis_text: Overall I enjoyed the experience I had playing this game, though it was different than I expected it to be. I think anyone going into this should expect it be more like a visual novel than anything else. I feel like it's got something it's trying to be but doesn't really hit the mark. The art style and music aren't quite cozy and the dialogue goes from nearing cringe territory to quite hard hitting. The end gets very long as it repeats the scenes over and over again with slight variations and I didn't totally feel like it had been earned yet. I've seen other reviews complaining that the story is very linear, but I don't see that as a negative. Not every story needs explorations and million different endings and a billion things to do. If you want to play those games, then avoid this one and go play those. The combat only gets interesting in the end-game. It feels like it was added on and not intended for this game. I did find the mechanics a bit interesting but for the most part it's pretty simple to sort out a strategy that works most of the time. When they started throwing new things at me in the end-game it only took two or three tried to get the right combo/luck.

title: Meg's Monster
analysis_text: A heartfelt story that visually might be very reminiscent of another game that features monster and human tensions, but it stands out with a nice focus on a set main cast that I couldn't help but just adore. Pretty good Pixel art, nice colour palettes that set the mood. With a mix of overworld sprites and more detailed combat sprites, the latter while not being the most animated compared to the former, I welcomed them to break the story from time to time. Combat. Every fight being unique, going the route of every fight is a boss rather than a random enemy. Most if not all of the fights have a unique THING going on to try and not be a repetitive turn based game, this is more expanded on in later fights Beautiful soundtrack, hitting the right notes in the correct places, though I felt it's a little limited and not too memorable, but that's purely personal. The combat feels a little tagged on, while there is variety in the enemies you typically only fight once, game overs tend to fall down to extremely bad luck since you are on a linear path with no real options besides your established mechanics. How the player avoids a game over, I'd say it's at least unique, so a bonus for that. Despite having a world map, the game is purely linear (you are pretty much locked into your linear route too) With no real reason to explore any place further outside of areas being no more than 2-3 rooms large at most points. Side quests don't really add much bulk to the game play or plot, with one side quest being awkwardly placed tone wise and the other being multiple side quests that seem almost shoe-horned in to bulk up the plot and twist (or someone just REALLY liked a certain character idk lol) While I think the ending is certainly a nice one, some elements of the plot and characters could've been explored more, the setting of the world REALLY should've been explored more, certain plot points I have either missed or the game didn't bother to tell me. (If it's left up to interpretation then that's totally fine) I feel the game could've just been MORE that what it already is if it was given more time to work on rather than a nice little shortened story to get done in a few hours. Despite what I feel, I do think it was a cute little game, However I would REALLY recommend one buys it SUPER discounted or just watch someone else play it, you will both share the same experience. I just don't think the price is worth a 5-7 hour experience. I'd like to recommend it but it's just lacking in content and replayability.

title: Meg's Monster
analysis_text: A heartwarming story, I cried. Twice. It'll feel good. Keep in mind two things if you come to play this game. First is that this is more of a visual novel than an RPG. I wouldn't call the combat system shallow, in that it's not a button masher and you will have to think. but don't expect deep combat. Approach each fight like a puzzle. The second thing is the story gets... I wouldn't say convoluted. But it does get a little dense, the same way a peanut butter is packed with calories; you might not realize how filling it is if you're not paying attention. The last 3rd of the story gets pretty bizarre to follow, and may require to suspend some disbelief. You'll have to take the game's word that sometimes there's a little magic that just goes unexplained in the world.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: Playing this game was an experience I will never forget! :D The art and music draws you in, but the comradery between Isabeau, Odile, Mirabelle, Bonnie, and Siffrin as well as the twists and turns along the way keep you locked in. I had so much fun just reading the dialogue between characters. So much humor and charm behind nearly every interaction, even with the people in the town. Their friendship is an anchor in a world of chaos, and it's so wholesome despite the pressure they faced. I also liked how the battle system was based on rock. paper, scissors, even if it did make combat less complex as a turn-based game. My only gripe with the battle system was how tedious it became to battle over the course of the game. I eventually found an item that allowed me to circumvent some of the tediousness which was nice. My main complaint with the game is that there are certain parts that feel unnecessarily frustrating and difficult to complete. I would say Act 4 gave me the most trouble and I actually had to go through a walkthrough twice in order to finally pass it. The story, characters, art, and music make it worth it but it does feel a little too much at certain points even if I understand it relates to a core part of the story. I highly recommend this game! This is one of those games that can change your life by playing. I will never forget my buddies Siffrin, Odile, Isabeau, Mirabelle, and Bonnie ; u; <3

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: If there one characteristic I'm certain on, In Stars And Time's writing takes out many dialogue flourishes and facial expressions to make the characters WORK, especially across many, many, many, loops. Those interactions changing across the loops is how I see this story suits itself to a game. On the flipside, I not so sure I felt like gameplay should really take this long, owning to how combat is "required" with a certain fast traveling resource that feels somehow separate from the story, and yet is part of the story. I suppose that resource is just-- not gelling with the story in a game technical sense. I suppose, the story doesn't have much interactions with that resource outside of the resource being used to force the player to battle enemies? Except, enemies aren't *the* problem, rather it is the environment that acts as the challenge posed by the story. Enemies are just there, with very little interactions compared to the environment. With that said, I enjoyed In Stars And Times for bringing out these lovable dorks of main party, and an excellent showcase of dialogue tricks... Oh, I suppose I should say the game does a lot with very little in regards to maps & music. Classic pitch shifting, hahaha!

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: This is a really good game and I'd recommend giving it a chance! The story is good, even if it is somewhat predictable. The characters were mostly likeable. The combat is turn-based with a simple yet fun action cost economy. You can somewhat customize your party with their own individual skill tree that you can change on the fly, and for free, to fit the situation you are in or just prefer. There are no random encounters in the traditional sense, all fights are set which, to me, gives off a DnD-esque feel. My only real criticism would be that I wanted the game to be longer, more side areas to explore, as the game felt short. Don't get me wrong, the game doesn't feel rushed but I just wanted more.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Very solid and fun RPG. Characters are lovable with cute designs and great writing with fun moments for all of the main party members and their various acquaintances. The game also does not hide its inspirations at all which can be pretty funny (such as the buff that the main character can apply to themselves after the prologue lol) It is a bit on the shorter side for an RPG, but it also doesn't waste your time with any grinding or tedious sidequests. Every fight you get into is relevant to the main story at hand, and you usually only have a handful of fights before you get to the next big Boss Fight. And the Bosses are universally really fun, usually sporting their own unique gimmicks to set each of those fights apart from each other. The side quests that do exist are few, but again, they don't waste your time and are very fun individual quests. The levelup system is also pretty simple too, but it gives you a good few ways to lean each of the characters in different directions. So I do feel like there's a good bit of agency. And I also love how the item system works, where once you get a consumable that can heal you or cure a status effect or something, you can just equip it to a party member, and then that person can always use that item once per fight, so you don't have to worry about running out of them or anything like that. My one complaint about the game is that I felt like by the end I got a bit too powerful for the game to handle. If you do all of the sidequests to unlock everyone's ultimate abilities, you can kinda become absurdly unstoppable and as a result the final boss was a little underwhelming since I was able to just blow right through it while barely taking any damage to my party. Other than that, like I said the game is fairly short, and I certainly wouldn't have complained if there were maybe 1 or 2 more seasons worth of content with a couple more story arcs to go through, but when my biggest complaint with a game is that I want more of it, that's usually a good sign. Overall very much worth the price of admission, and in many ways I think is also a good intro RPG to the genre if you're not as familiar with its conventions. But even as a long time fan of RPGs I still loved what it had to offer.
